1156.title: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1156.word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1156.hook: two in the morning in a temple courtyard: the hardest hour, and a song that wakes everyone up
1156.carry: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1156.tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1156.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri, Hindus who keep the jagarana stay awake through the night, in temples or at home, with bhajans, chanting of Om Namah Shivaya, and rounds of worship of the linga until dawn.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum, the fast: it clears space and turns each pang into a bell. A new week begins, and the night goes on.
screen: `THE FAST: HUNGER AS A BELL.` · `A NEW WEEK, THE SAME NIGHT.`

segments.voice: A little before two in the morning, in a temple courtyard. The crowd that pushed through the gates at sunset has thinned. A child sleeps across her grandmother's lap. A man in a shawl keeps nodding, catching himself, nodding again. Even the drummer looks tired. Hours like this decide whether a vigil is kept or quietly given up. Then somebody near the shrine starts a new song, loud, with a call everyone knows how to answer. Heads lift. The man in the shawl sits up and sings.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `THE HARDEST HOUR.` → `SOMEBODY STARTS A SONG.`

segments.voice: Keeping awake on this night is called jagarana, the vigil. It gives the night its character, and it's easy to misread as a test of endurance. Look at how it's done. First, together. In temples, singing, chanting and rounds of worship come one after another, so there's always something to wake into. You keep yourself awake, and the person next to you, and they keep you. Second, on purpose. People stay up all night for many reasons. The vigil asks you to stay up toward something, attention pointed at Shiva, hour after hour. Third, it points past the night. The Katha Upanishad has a call that fits this hour: arise, awake, go to the great teachers and learn. It warns that the path is as sharp as a razor's edge. That wakefulness isn't about eyelids. But staying awake on this one night is a way of rehearsing the other kind. So the courtyard at two in the morning is a small picture of the whole teaching. Everyone is tired. Nobody is awake by their own strength alone. And what lifts the heads isn't a scolding. It's a song someone was willing to start. Sometimes, in the hard hour, the lesson isn't to stay awake. It's to be the one who starts the song.
screen: `JAGARANA: THE VIGIL.` · `KEPT AWAKE TOGETHER.` · `AWAKE TOWARD SOMETHING.` · `ARISE, AWAKE, AND LEARN.` · then, large: `BE THE ONE WHO STARTS THE SONG.`

segments.voice: Sit a little straighter than usual, eyes just slightly open and resting on a spot in front of you, and when the mind starts to drift or dull, the way heads nod at two in the morning, don't scold yourself. Lift: straighten the back, take one fuller breath, and come back, because every lift is a small vigil. If you pray, you can let Om Namah Shivaya, or the name of God you use, be the song that lifts you.
Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Lesson three: jagarana, the vigil, wakefulness kept together and pointed toward Shiva, a rehearsal for waking up.
screen: `MAHA SHIVARATRI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Nobody stays awake alone. See you tomorrow.

1157.title: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1157.word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1157.hook: a string of rough brown beads moves through the fingers, one name per bead, hour after hour
1157.carry: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1157.tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1157.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri, some who keep the vigil do japa of Om Namah Shivaya, aloud, whispered or silently, counting on a rudraksha mala, alongside temple songs and worship through the night.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum, jagarana: the vigil, kept awake together, and the one who starts the song.
screen: `JAGARANA: AWAKE TOGETHER.` · `WHAT FILLS THE HOURS.`

segments.voice: Rough brown beads, a little uneven, each one wrinkled like a tiny walnut. They hang from the fingers of a woman sitting against a pillar. Her thumb draws one bead toward the palm, her lips move, and the next bead comes. She isn't reading, or singing with the crowd. She's saying one short phrase, once per bead, and has been for a long while. Around her the night goes on: songs rising and falling, the line to the shrine moving and stopping. Her beads keep their own slow time. Today's lesson: what you hold onto once you're up.
screen: `ROUGH BROWN BEADS.` → `ONE PHRASE PER BEAD.` → `WHAT YOU HOLD ONCE YOU'RE UP.`

segments.voice: The phrase is Om Namah Shivaya. Namah Shivaya is the Panchakshara, the five-syllable mantra: na, mah, shi, va, ya. You've met it this year: it's the line from deep inside the Rudram, salutation to Shiva, the kind one. The great Vedic hymn and the bead in a tired hand are joined by those five syllables. Saying a mantra over and over is japa, and the Shiva Purana praises this mantra at length. Here's why it suits this night. A long night needs something small. At ten in the evening a long hymn is easy to follow. At three in the morning it gets hard. But you can still hold five syllables. Japa is built for the hour when bigger things slip away. It can be said aloud, whispered, or held silently, so it works in a loud crowd and a quiet room. The beads matter too. They're rudraksha, and the Shiva Purana tells that these seeds came from Shiva's own tears. They keep count, so the mind doesn't have to, and give the hand a job, so the body stays in the practice when thoughts wander. When you notice you've drifted, there's a bead in your fingers, waiting. So the fourth lesson is a thread: through all the hours, one short name keeps running, the name the Rudram bowed to. The night is long. The thread is short enough to hold.
screen: `NAMAH SHIVAYA: FIVE SYLLABLES.` · `THE LINE FROM INSIDE THE RUDRAM.` · `JAPA: SMALL ENOUGH FOR 3 A.M.` · `RUDRAKSHA: BEADS FROM SHIVA'S TEARS.` · then, large: `A THREAD SHORT ENOUGH TO HOLD.`

segments.voice: Choose something short to repeat, one breath at a time: Om Namah Shivaya if you pray, or a name of God from your own tradition, or simply counting breaths from one to ten. If you have beads, or a string with knots, let the fingers move one at a time, and when you notice you've drifted, don't start over; just take the next bead, the next breath, the next word.
Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Lesson four: japa, the name repeated through the night, Om Namah Shivaya, a thread short enough to hold at three in the morning.

segments.voice: Your line: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Five syllables fit any hour. Until tomorrow.

1158.title: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1158.word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum

1158.carry: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1158.tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1158.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri, Hindus bring water, milk, bilva leaves and flowers to Shiva temples and offer them on the linga, sometimes waiting in line through the night; others offer them to a linga or image at home.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum, japa: Om Namah Shivaya on bead after bead, a thread short enough to hold.
screen: `JAPA: A THREAD THROUGH THE NIGHT.` · `WHAT GOES ON THE PLATE.`

segments.voice: The line for the shrine stretches past the gate and around the corner, and it's past midnight. Look at what people carry. A small steel plate. On it, a little pot of water or a cup of milk, a few green leaves picked that morning, a flower that grows wild by the road. In some places, a prickly fruit no one would ever eat. A student near the back has only a plastic bottle of water, and he holds it like it matters. Nobody here carries anything expensive.
screen: `A LINE PAST MIDNIGHT.` → `WATER, LEAVES, A WILD FLOWER.` → `NOTHING THAT COST MUCH.`

segments.voice: Start with the water, plain, poured over the linga the way the Rudram was chanted over it. Then the leaves: bilva, from a tree sacred to Shiva. The Shiva Purana praises worship with bilva, and on this night people lay bilva leaves on the stone. Then the wild things. In some places people bring flowers and fruits from the edges, the kinds no garden wants, because Shiva is pictured at the edges: the mountain, the cremation ground, the forest. What's striking is how little any of it costs. One of Shiva's names is Ashutosha, which people explain as the one who is quickly pleased. The tradition pictures him delighted by a leaf and a little water given with care. The Bhagavad Gita says something close, in Krishna's voice: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, offered with devotion, is accepted. So the offering isn't a payment. It's a way of putting attention into your hands. You pick the leaf, carry it, wait in line, and set it down with the name on your lips. Everything is small so the care can be large. Then the water runs off, and before long the leaves are cleared away. Nothing is kept. The offering is meant to be given completely, and let go. That's the fifth lesson of the night: not how much you bring, but how fully you put it down.
screen: `WATER, POURED FIRST.` · `BILVA, LEAVES SACRED TO SHIVA.` · `ASHUTOSHA: QUICKLY PLEASED.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.` · then, large: `SMALL, SO THE CARE CAN BE LARGE.`

segments.voice: Pour a little water into a cup if there's some nearby, or just rest your open hands in your lap, and think of the smallest thing you could give today: a minute of real listening, a kind word you've been holding back. Hold it for a few breaths, then slowly put it down, as if setting a leaf on a stone. If you pray, you can offer it with Shiva's name, or the name of God you use.
Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Lesson five: the offering, water, bilva and wild flowers, small so the care can be large, and given away completely.

1159.title: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1159.word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1159.hook: gray light over the temple roof, one last worship, and food handed to someone else before the fast is broken
1159.carry: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1159.howItsDone: The morning after Maha Shivaratri, those who kept the fast worship again, may give food or gifts, and then break the fast with a simple meal; temples may distribute prasad to the people who kept the night.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum, the offering: water, bilva, a wild flower, small so the care can be large. Today the night ends, and so does this part of the path.
screen: `THE OFFERING, SET DOWN.` · `THE NIGHT ENDS.`

segments.voice: The sky over the temple roof goes from black to slate to a thin gray. Birds start before anyone else. People who have been up all night stand, stretch, wince, and gather for one last round of worship. The bell rings. The lamp is waved. Then a woman near the gate unties a cloth bundle she's carried since yesterday. There's food inside, and she has fasted a full day. She hands it out first, to the people beside her, to the man sweeping the steps. Only then does she take a bite.
screen: `BLACK, SLATE, GRAY.` → `ONE LAST WORSHIP.` → `FOOD HANDED OUT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Breaking a fast at the right time is called parana. In the Shiva Purana's account of the vow, the night doesn't end with the last song. The next morning brings worship again, and giving, and only then is the fast broken. The vow closes the way it opened, on purpose. That ending matters. A night like this can turn into a story you tell about yourself: I stayed up, I didn't eat. The morning undoes that. It sends you back to ordinary things, food, a tired body, other people's hunger, and asks you to bring the night with you. If the night was about attention, the morning is where it's tested. The whole course: a resolve, a fast, a vigil, a name, an offering, and a morning that hands the night back to ordinary life. It closes the Shiva part of the path too. We read selections of the Shiva Purana: the pillar no one could measure, Sati who would not hear him mocked, Parvati's tapas. We stood before Nataraja, the dancer, walked through the Shiva Sahasranama, opened Kashmir Shaivism through the Shiva Sutras, lived inside the Rudram, and kept one great night. Tomorrow the path turns from a god to a way of thinking: the six darshanas, schools of Hindu thought, set side by side and never ranked. First, Nyaya, the school of logic.
screen: `PARANA: BREAKING THE FAST.` · `WORSHIP, GIVING, THEN FOOD.` · `THE MORNING TESTS THE NIGHT.` · `THE SHIVA PART, GATHERED UP.` · then, large: `BRING THE NIGHT WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Sit as if the night has just ended and the light is coming up, and walk back slowly through its lessons: the resolve, the fast, the vigil, the name, the offering. Hold the one that stayed with you, and let it go with you into the first ordinary thing you'll do after this sit. If you pray, you can give thanks to Shiva, or to the God you know, for the night.
Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. The last lesson: parana, the morning, when worship and giving come first and the fast is broken.

1160.title: Nyaya (logic)
1160.hook: the forecast says rain, the sky says no, a neighbor says no, a knee says yes: how do you know anything?
1160.howItsDone: In traditional Sanskrit learning, students study Nyaya through the Nyaya Sutra and its commentaries, beginning with the means of knowing and learning to test an argument with a teacher.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SIXTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum came to dawn: worship, giving, then breaking the fast. The Shiva part of the path closed with it.
screen: `THE NIGHT ENDS AT DAWN.` · `A NEW PART BEGINS.`

segments.voice: The weather app says rain at four. You look up: clear blue sky. Your neighbor, who has watched this sky for decades, says it won't rain today, not with that wind. And your knee aches the way it does before a storm. Four voices, and they don't agree. Which do you trust? Underneath sits a bigger question: when you say you know something, where did that knowing come from? A school of Hindu thought made that question its starting point.
screen: `THE APP SAYS RAIN.` → `THE SKY SAYS NO.` → `HOW DO YOU KNOW ANYTHING?`

segments.voice: This part of the path is the six darshanas. Darshana means seeing, and here a way of seeing: a school of thought. We'll take them one at a time, side by side, and rank none of them. Nyaya comes first only because we have to start somewhere. Nyaya is the school of logic. Its root text, the Nyaya Sutra, is traditionally credited to a sage named Gautama, and it opens with a list of what it will examine. The very first is pramana: a means of knowing, a way real knowledge reaches you. It names four. Perception: what you see, hear and touch yourself, the clear sky. Inference: reasoning from a sign to what you can't see, the knee that aches before rain. Comparison: knowing a new thing by its likeness to one you know. The commentators' example is a traveler told that a certain forest animal looks like a cow, who recognizes it when he meets it. And word: the testimony of someone reliable, the neighbor who has read this sky for years. Here's the surprise. Near its start, this book of logic says its aim is release, freedom from suffering. False knowledge leads to faults, faults to action, action to birth, birth to suffering. Remove the false knowledge at the bottom and the whole chain comes loose. For Nyaya, thinking clearly isn't the opposite of a spiritual life. It's one of its paths, and it starts with one question: how do I know this?
screen: `DARSHANA: A WAY OF SEEING.` · `PRAMANA: A MEANS OF KNOWING.` · `SEE, INFER, COMPARE, BE TOLD.` · `CLEAR THINKING AS A PATH.` · then, large: `HOW DO I KNOW THIS?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you're sure of today, about a person, about tomorrow, about yourself, and ask quietly where it came from: did you see it, reason to it from a sign, match it to something you knew, or were you told, and by someone how reliable? Don't argue with it; just find its source, and notice whether its sources agree. If you pray, you can ask the God you know for clear sight.
Nyaya. The school of logic, which begins by asking how we know, names four means of knowing, and says the goal of clear thinking is freedom from suffering.

1161.title: Nyaya (logic)
1161.hook: a gray column rises behind the next hill, nobody can see a flame, and everybody says fire
1161.howItsDone: In traditional Sanskrit study, students of Nyaya learn inference through the example of smoke and fire on a hill, practicing how to state a sign, a rule and a supporting case, and how to spot reasons that only look like reasons.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nyaya opened with four means of knowing: perception, inference, comparison, and the word of someone reliable. Today, one of the four, up close.
screen: `NYAYA: FOUR MEANS OF KNOWING.` · `ONE OF THEM, UP CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Three friends walk a ridge in the late afternoon. Across the valley, from behind the next hill, a gray column is rising, leaning with the wind. Nobody can see a flame; the hill is in the way. Yet all three say the same word at once: fire. Nobody stops to wonder how they knew a thing none of them can see. Nyaya stops right there. That quick leap is one of its four means of knowing, and the hill with smoke on it is the example its teachers reach for.
screen: `A GRAY COLUMN, NO FLAME.` → `ALL THREE SAY FIRE.` → `HOW DID THEY KNOW?`

segments.voice: The word is anumana: inference, knowing something you can't see by way of a sign you can. Nyaya teachers lay it out in plain pieces. The hill has fire, because it has smoke. What makes that work: smoke and fire have been seen together before, at the kitchen hearth, again and again. The opposite has been seen too: a still lake, no fire, no smoke. From cases like those comes a rule: wherever there's smoke, there's fire. Later Nyaya teachers named that rule vyapti, pervasion: smoke is always found inside the territory of fire. With the rule in hand, the leap isn't a guess. It's knowing. But Nyaya cares just as much how the leap goes wrong. The Nyaya Sutra names reasons that only look like reasons, and teachers give homely examples. One trap: the sign isn't what you think. That gray column might be mist off the trees, or dust from a road. Before you reason from smoke, make sure it's smoke. A second trap: the rule run backward. Wherever there's fire, there's smoke? A red-hot iron ball glows with fire and gives off no smoke. The rule runs one way. These traps turn up everywhere. A closed office door, so the boss is angry. A short reply, so they don't care. Maybe. Or maybe it's mist. Nyaya doesn't ask you to stop inferring; you couldn't live a day without it. It asks two questions first: is the sign real, and does the rule really run this way?
screen: `ANUMANA: FROM A SIGN TO THE UNSEEN.` · `SMOKE AND FIRE AT THE HEARTH.` · `IS IT SMOKE, OR MIST?` · `THE RULE RUNS ONE WAY.` · then, large: `IS THE SIGN REAL?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a conclusion you reached this week about someone from a sign, a look, a silence, a tone of voice, and ask: was it really what I took it for, or could it have been mist? Then ask whether you know this sign always comes with that meaning. Don't decide anything; just let the leap slow down until you can see it, and if you pray, ask the God you know for clear eyes.
Nyaya. Today, anumana, inference: the hill has fire because it has smoke, as long as it's really smoke, and the rule really runs that way.
screen: `NYAYA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Nyaya, logic. Is it smoke, or is it mist? See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1161 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NYAYA (LOGIC).`

1162.title: Nyaya (logic)
1162.hook: a bell is struck and fades, and a Nyaya teacher turns that fading into an argument in five steps
1162.howItsDone: In traditional Sanskrit schools, students meet Nyaya through the Nyaya Sutra and its commentaries, learning to set out an argument step by step and to test it in discussion with a teacher.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: This week began with the long night of Maha Shivaratri, then turned to the six darshanas, schools of thought never ranked. Yesterday brought Nyaya, logic. Today closes the week.
screen: `FROM SHIVA'S NIGHT TO THE SIX SCHOOLS.` · `NYAYA, CONTINUED.`

segments.voice: Somebody strikes a bell. The note blooms out into the room, hangs there, thins, and then it's gone. Nobody is surprised. Of course it faded. But a teacher of Nyaya would stop you right there: how do you know it had to fade? You heard this one bell, not every sound there will ever be. Nyaya takes that small, ordinary leap and slows it down until you can see every step. Today, one of its tools: an argument in five parts, said out loud, so the other person can check each one.
screen: `A BELL, AND THEN SILENCE.` → `HOW DO YOU KNOW IT HAD TO FADE?` → `AN ARGUMENT IN FIVE PARTS.`

segments.voice: The Nyaya Sutra names the five parts: the proposition, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion. Its early commentator, Vatsyayana, walks them through with sound itself. One: sound does not last. Two: because it is produced. Three: whatever is produced does not last, like a clay pot. Four: sound, too, is produced. Five: so sound does not last. It sounds slow, even a little silly. But look at step three, because that's where the whole thing lives. It names the rule out loud, then points to a case both people have seen with their own eyes. Pots get made, and pots break. An argument in Nyaya isn't one mind talking to itself. It's two people looking at the same pot. If you can't point to a shared case where your rule plainly holds, the argument doesn't stand. And because the rule is said out loud, the other person can test it. Not everyone agreed with this one. Thinkers of the Mimamsa school held that the sounds of the Veda are eternal, and they argued the point with Nyaya. Nyaya's answer wasn't to shout louder. It was to lay out the steps, so the disagreement could land on the step where it really lived. Now bring it home. A friend doesn't text back. One: they're upset with me. Two: because they haven't answered. Three: whoever doesn't answer is upset, like… and there you stop. Where's your pot?
screen: `FIVE PARTS, SAID OUT LOUD.` · `SOUND DOESN'T LAST, LIKE A POT.` · `THE EXAMPLE DOES THE REAL WORK.` · `NAME THE STEP YOU DISAGREE WITH.` · then, large: `WHERE'S YOUR POT?`

segments.voice: Listen to one sound, a chime if you have one, or whatever comes next, and follow it all the way down into quiet. Then hold up one rule of thumb you live by, like anyone who's late doesn't care, and look for its pot: one real case where it plainly held, and one where it didn't. If you pray, you can rest in the name of God you use as the silence settles.
Nyaya. The school of logic, and its argument in five parts: a claim, a reason, an example you can both see, the fit, and the conclusion.
screen: `NYAYA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Nyaya, logic. A good reason can point to its pot. I'll be here tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1162 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NYAYA (LOGIC).`
